**On Margins**

There is a kind of freedom that lives in the margin.

Not the center, where the official text sits in its tidy rows, making promises and stating facts. Not the headline, bold and certain. But the blank space beside it—the narrow white strip where someone might once have written *yes*, or *doubtful*, or *this reminded me of rain*, or *I was here*.

Margins are often treated as leftovers, as if meaning only exists where it has been approved and printed. But I find myself drawn to the edges: the notes left in library books, the doodles in the corner of a notebook, the pause between one sentence and the next, the place where a thought hasn’t yet decided what shape to take.

A page with wide margins feels like an invitation. It says: you may respond. You may disagree. You may add something small and private that no one else will understand for years, if ever. Writing in the margin is a humble act. It does not pretend to replace the main text. It simply insists that reading is not passive, that understanding is not a one-way street, that even the most finished-looking idea may still have room for a whisper.

I think a lot of life happens in margins.

The real conversation often begins after the formal one ends. The truth sometimes appears in the aside, the joke, the hesitation, the thing almost said. A person’s character can reveal itself not in grand declarations but in how they treat the unimportant moments: waiting in line, listening to someone boring, deciding whether to be kind when no one is watching. Margins are where performance relaxes.

Even memory works this way. The major events—graduations, moves, losses, celebrations—are the printed text of a life. But what returns most often are the marginal details: the smell of a hallway, a particular blue cup, the way light fell across a kitchen table, a sentence overheard on a train. These fragments seem minor, yet they carry enormous emotional weight. They are the annotations our lives leave on us.

There is also freedom in literal margins: sidewalks, shorelines, borders, the edge of a forest where trees thin into field. Such places belong partly to one world and partly to another. They are not fully inside, not fully outside. They can feel unsettling, but also generative. Many new things begin at edges, where old categories loosen and something less named becomes possible.

Perhaps that is why I like the idea of writing freely. Not because freedom means having no structure, but because structure gives freedom something to press against. A river needs banks; otherwise it is just a puddle. A poem needs form; otherwise the words may scatter. Even a blank page, for all its openness, asks for a beginning.

So if I were to write freely, I would not try to escape the margins. I would live in them a little. I would notice what grows there: questions, half-formed hopes, strange connections, quiet corrections. I would leave space for response. I would remember that not everything important needs to be centered to matter.

Sometimes the most honest thing a person can say is not the polished statement, but the small note written beside it:

*I wasn’t sure.  
But I kept going.*
